name: Sicily
tagline: Greek temples, Arab-Norman gold, a smoking volcano and the best pastry in Italy.
intro: The Mediterranean's largest island has been Greek, Roman, Arab, Norman, Spanish and Bourbon, and it shows in its stones and on its plates. Doric temples stand in almond orchards at Agrigento, Byzantine mosaics glitter in Palermo and Monreale, and whole towns in the southeast were rebuilt in honey-coloured baroque after the earthquake of 1693. Over it all, Etna smokes and rumbles.

Sicily feels like a small continent. Palermo is chaotic and magnificent, with street markets that smell of fried chickpea fritters and lemons. Catania is black lava stone and loud fish markets. Off the coast lie volcanic Aeolian islands, the Egadi, and Pantelleria, closer to Tunisia than to Palermo. Breakfast is granita with a brioche; dessert might be a cannolo filled to order. Allow more time than you think.

hero_image.alt: The little island of Isola Bella joined to the shore by a sandbar in a turquoise bay below Taormina
hero_image.credit: Solomonn Levi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

best_time: April to June and September to October are best, warm enough to swim from May. Easter brings remarkable processions; July and August are very hot, especially inland, and winters are mild on the coast.
getting_there: Fly into Palermo or Catania, with smaller airports at Trapani and Comiso. Trains are slow but useful between the main cities; regional buses fill the gaps, and a car is best for the interior and the southeast. Ferries arrive from Naples, Genoa and Civitavecchia, and hydrofoils serve the Aeolian Islands from Milazzo and the Egadi from Trapani.

places.name: Palermo
places.desc: A gloriously messy capital of Arab domes, baroque churches and street food. See the golden mosaics of the Cappella Palatina, the red domes of San Giovanni degli Eremiti and the cathedral, then lose yourself in the Ballarò and Vucciria markets. Take bus 389 up to Monreale cathedral for more mosaics, and the beach at Mondello.

image.alt: The gold Byzantine mosaics and painted wooden ceiling inside the Cappella Palatina in Palermo
image.credit: Pistillo99, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

places.name: Taormina
places.desc: A clifftop resort above the Ionian with one of the world's most dramatic theatres: the ancient Greek theatre, with Etna as its backdrop. Walk Corso Umberto, climb to Castelmola for an almond wine, and take the cable car down to swim at Isola Bella.

image.alt: The curved stone seats and ruined stage of the Greek theatre of Taormina above the sea
image.credit: Solomonn Levi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

places.name: Mount Etna
places.desc: Europe's tallest active volcano, at around 3,300 metres. A cable car and 4x4s from Rifugio Sapienza take you close to the summit craters with a guide; lower down, walk through old lava flows and the Silvestri craters, then taste Etna Rosso and Carricante at a winery on the north slope.

image.alt: Mount Etna sending a plume of smoke into a golden evening sky, seen from Taormina
image.credit: Solomonn Levi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

places.name: Syracuse and Ortigia
places.desc: Once the greatest city in the Greek world, Syracuse has a vast Greek theatre and the 'Ear of Dionysius' cave in its archaeological park. Its island heart, Ortigia, is a maze of baroque palazzi around a cathedral built into a Greek temple of Athena. Swim off the rocks below the sea walls.

image.alt: The waterfront houses of Ortigia rising from the sea in Syracuse
image.credit: Ввласенко, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

places.name: Valley of the Temples
places.desc: A ridge outside Agrigento lined with Greek temples, including the Temple of Concordia, among the best-preserved Doric temples anywhere. Come at the end of the day, when the stone turns gold, and walk on to the Kolymbethra garden of citrus and almonds below.

image.alt: The Doric Temple of Concordia in the Valley of the Temples at Agrigento under a blue sky
image.credit: Berthold Werner, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

places.name: Noto and the Val di Noto
places.desc: Noto was rebuilt after the 1693 earthquake as a stage set of golden baroque, best seen from the steps of San Nicolò cathedral at dusk. Nearby Modica tumbles down a ravine and makes grainy chocolate, and Ragusa Ibla is a hilltop of domes and palazzi. All are UNESCO-listed.

image.alt: The baroque cathedral of San Nicolò in Noto at the top of a broad stone staircase
image.credit: Berthold Werner, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

things_to_do.title: Eat your way through Ballarò
things_to_do.desc: Palermo's oldest market is street food heaven: panelle and crocchè in bread, sfincione, boiled octopus and, for the brave, pani ca' meusa, a bun of spleen. Go in the morning when it's busiest.

things_to_do.title: See an Opera dei Pupi show
things_to_do.desc: Watch knights in tin armour fight Saracens in a puppet theatre in Palermo. The Cuticchio family's Teatro dei Pupi on Via Bara all'Olivella keeps the tradition alive.

things_to_do.title: Climb Stromboli at sunset
things_to_do.desc: With a licensed guide, hike up the volcano in the late afternoon to watch eruptions from a viewing point at dusk, then head down by torchlight. Book well ahead in summer.

things_to_do.title: Watch sunset at the Trapani salt pans
things_to_do.desc: Between Trapani and Marsala, windmills stand over shimmering salt pans that turn pink at sunset. Take the little boat to the island of Mozia, a Phoenician town.

things_to_do.title: Walk the Riserva dello Zingaro
things_to_do.desc: Sicily's first nature reserve: a cliff path of about seven kilometres between San Vito Lo Capo and Scopello, with steps down to pebble coves of very clear water.

things_to_do.title: Visit Segesta
things_to_do.desc: An unfinished Doric temple alone on a hillside, and a Greek theatre higher up with views to the sea. It is one of the most atmospheric ancient sites in Italy.

things_to_do.title: Watch a Greek tragedy in Syracuse
things_to_do.desc: Every spring and early summer, the INDA foundation stages classical Greek drama in the ancient theatre of Syracuse, where Aeschylus once premiered plays. Sit on the stone seats as the sun goes down.

things_to_do.title: Swim at the Vendicari reserve
things_to_do.desc: South of Noto, a protected coast of lagoons with flamingos, a ruined tuna fishery and long sandy beaches such as Calamosche. Bring water and shade: there are no facilities.

flavours.name: Arancine
flavours.desc: Fried rice balls stuffed with meat ragù or ham and mozzarella. In Palermo they're round and feminine (arancina); in Catania, cone-shaped and masculine (arancino).

flavours.name: Cannolo
flavours.desc: A crisp fried pastry tube filled with sweetened sheep's ricotta, sometimes with candied orange or pistachio. Good shops fill them to order.

flavours.name: Granita with brioche
flavours.desc: A summer breakfast: almond, lemon, coffee or black mulberry granita with a soft brioche for dipping. Catania and Messina do it best.

flavours.name: Cassata siciliana
flavours.desc: A baroque cake of sponge, ricotta cream and marzipan, covered in icing and candied fruit. Traditionally made at Easter.

flavours.name: Pasta alla Norma
flavours.desc: Catania's classic: pasta with fried aubergine, tomato sauce, basil and grated salted ricotta. Named after Bellini's opera.

flavours.name: Pasta con le sarde
flavours.desc: A Palermo dish of fresh sardines, wild fennel, pine nuts, raisins and saffron, topped with toasted breadcrumbs. Arab influence in a bowl.

flavours.name: Pistacchio di Bronte DOP
flavours.desc: Bright green pistachios grown on Etna's lava slopes, harvested every other year and used in pesto, gelato and pastries.

flavours.name: Cioccolato di Modica IGP
flavours.desc: Cold-worked chocolate with a grainy texture from undissolved sugar crystals, made following a method inherited from Spanish rule. Try the chilli or cinnamon versions.

flavours.name: Nero d'Avola and Etna Rosso
flavours.desc: Nero d'Avola gives rich, dark reds in the south; Nerello Mascalese on the slopes of Etna makes elegant, mineral reds that wine critics love.

flavours.name: Marsala and Passito di Pantelleria
flavours.desc: Marsala is a fortified wine from the west coast; Pantelleria's sweet passito, made from sun-dried Zibibbo grapes, tastes of apricots and honey.

legacy_restaurants.name: Antica Focacceria San Francesco
legacy_restaurants.desc: A Palermo institution of marble tables and cast-iron details opposite the church of San Francesco. Order pani ca' meusa, panelle, arancine and sfincione.

legacy_restaurants.name: Antico Caffè Spinnato
legacy_restaurants.desc: The grand café of Via Principe di Belmonte, with tables on the pedestrian street. Come for cannoli, cassata and a granita in summer.

legacy_restaurants.name: Caffè Sicilia
legacy_restaurants.desc: The Assenza family's pastry shop on Corso Vittorio Emanuele, now famous through chef Corrado Assenza. Try the almond granita, the cassata and anything with local citrus or honey.

legacy_restaurants.name: Antica Dolceria Bonajuto
legacy_restaurants.desc: Sicily's oldest chocolate maker, on Corso Umberto I, still working cocoa cold in the old way. Taste chocolate with vanilla or chilli and the 'mpanatigghi, pastries filled with chocolate and minced beef.

stay_local.title: A cooking school on a wine estate
stay_local.desc: Anna Tasca Lanza's school at Case Vecchie, on the Regaleali estate in the hills between Palermo and Caltanissetta, offers stays with classes in the farmhouse kitchen, using produce from the gardens.

stay_local.title: A farm stay on the slopes of Etna
stay_local.desc: Monaci delle Terre Nere, near Zafferana Etnea, is a 19th-century manor surrounded by organic orchards, vineyards and old lava walls, with a restaurant that cooks from the farm and views to the sea.

stay_local.title: A dammuso on Pantelleria
stay_local.desc: Rent a dammuso, the island's traditional domed house of thick black lava stone, with a walled garden built to protect a single orange tree from the wind. Many are run by island families as holiday homes.

stay_local.title: A family-run hotel on Salina
stay_local.desc: The greenest Aeolian island has small hotels run by local families, often among caper fields and vines of Malvasia. Evenings are for granita in Lingua and sunsets over the sea at Pollara.

day_trips.desc: A beach town below a great rock, with a Norman cathedral whose apse holds a stunning mosaic of Christ Pantocrator. Swim right below the old town.

day_trips.how: 1h by car or bus to Rifugio Sapienza
day_trips.desc: Go up to the craters by cable car and 4x4, or walk the Silvestri craters, then stop for wine on the way back.
Rent a bike and ride to Cala Rossa and Bue Marino, then see the old tuna fishery, the Ex Stabilimento Florio.
See the golden baroque centre, eat almond granita at Caffè Sicilia, and finish the day with a swim at the Vendicari reserve just to the south.

hidden_gems.name: Salina
hidden_gems.desc: The quietest and greenest of the Aeolian Islands, two extinct volcanoes covered in vines and capers. Watch sunset from Pollara, where Il Postino was filmed, and taste Malvasia delle Lipari at a family winery.

image.alt: The twin green volcanic peaks of Salina rising from a deep blue sea
image.credit: Carsten Steger, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

hidden_gems.name: Scicli
hidden_gems.desc: A baroque town in a ravine in the southeast, less visited than Noto or Ragusa but just as lovely. It is the setting of the Inspector Montalbano TV series; the town hall is his police station.

image.alt: Baroque palazzi and café tables along Via Francesco Mormino Penna in Scicli
image.credit: Julian Lupyan, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

hidden_gems.name: Marettimo
hidden_gems.desc: The wildest of the Egadi islands, with no cars, mountain trails among wild rosemary and sea caves all around its coast. Local fishermen take visitors round the island by boat, stopping to swim.

image.alt: A small cove of clear blue water below rocky slopes on Marettimo
image.credit: Salvo Cannizzaro, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

hidden_gems.name: Erice
hidden_gems.desc: A medieval walled town 750 metres up a mountain above Trapani, often wrapped in mist. Take the cable car up, try the almond pastries at Maria Grammatico, and look down on the salt pans and the Egadi.

image.alt: The Gothic stone façade of the Chiesa Madre in the hill town of Erice
image.credit: Berthold Werner, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

festivals.name: Festa di Sant'Agata
festivals.desc: One of the biggest religious festivals in the world: hundreds of thousands of people in white tunics pull the saint's silver reliquary through the city for days, with giant candles and fireworks.

festivals.name: U Fistinu di Santa Rosalia
festivals.desc: A huge triumphal cart carries the saint's statue from the cathedral down the Cassaro to the sea, ending with fireworks over the Foro Italico.

festivals.name: Processione dei Misteri
festivals.desc: Twenty groups of 18th-century wooden statues depicting the Passion are carried through the streets for about 24 hours by members of the city's ancient guilds.

festivals.name: Infiorata di Noto
festivals.desc: Via Corrado Nicolaci is carpeted with huge designs made of flower petals, under the baroque balconies of Palazzo Nicolaci, with a different theme each year.

culture: Sicily's Opera dei Pupi, puppet theatre telling the tales of Charlemagne's paladins, is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list; Palermo's puppets are smaller and lighter, Catania's large and heavy. Painted carts, the carretti siciliani, once carried the same stories on their sides, and cantastorie storytellers sang them in the squares. Caltagirone's 142-step staircase is faced in majolica tiles, and Sicilian, a language of its own, mixes Greek, Arabic, Norman and Spanish words. Holy Week is intense, the marranzano jaw harp twangs at folk festivals, and literature runs from Verga and Pirandello to Lampedusa's The Leopard.
